q.e: True Course is the intended path of the aircraft over the ground, measured clockwise starting from True (Geographic) North.

q.t: Given: TC: 183°; WCA: +011°; MH: 198°; CH: 200°. What are TH and VAR?
q.e: TH = TC + WCA = 183 + 11 = 194°. VAR = TH - MH = 194 - 198 = -4°, which is 4° West.

q.t: Given: TC: 183°; WCA: +011°; MH: 198°; CH: 200°. What are the TH and the DEV?
Given: TC: 183°; WCA: +011°; MH: 198°; CH: 200°. What are the VAR and the DEV?
Where does the inclination reach its lowest value?
q.e: Magnetic inclination (dip) is the angle the magnetic field lines make with the surface. It is 0 degrees (absolute lowest value) precisely at the magnetic equator.

q.t: The angle between compass north and magnetic north is called...
q.e: Deviation is the localized error induced by the aircraft's own metals and electronic fields, creating a discrepancy between Magnetic North and Compass North.

q.t: Which direction corresponds to 'compass north' (CN)?
o: The most northerly part of the magnetic compass in the aircraft, where the reading takes place
The direction to which the direct reading compass aligns due to earth's and aircraft's magnetic fields
The angle between the aircraft heading and magnetic north
The direction from an arbitrary point on Earth to the geographical North Pole
q.e: Compass North is the actual, uncorrected direction the needle points, influenced simultaneously by both the Earth's magnetic field and the aircraft's magnetic deviation.

q.t: The term 'isogonal' or 'isogonic line' is defined as a line on an aeronautical chart, connecting all points with the same value of...
q.e: Isogonic lines connect points of equal magnetic variation on a map, helping pilots apply correct variation corrections for different regions.

q.t: The term 'agonic line' is defined as a line on Earth or an aeronautical chart, connecting all points with the...
q.e: An agonic line is a specialized isogonic line connecting all points where the magnetic variation is exactly zero degrees (True North and Magnetic North align perfectly).

q.t: Which are the official basic units for horizontal distances used in aeronautical navigation and their abbreviations?
q.e: Standard ICAO aviation navigation primarily uses Nautical Miles (NM) for horizontal distance, though kilometers (km) are also officially recognised and used in certain contexts/countries.

q.t: 1000 ft equal...
q.e: One foot is approximately 0.3048 meters. Therefore, 1000 feet is roughly equal to 304.8 meters, which is rounded to 300 meters in general operational terms.

q.t: 5500 m equal...
q.e: 1 meter is roughly 3.28 feet. 5500 meters * 3.28 = 18,040 feet, heavily rounded to 18,000 ft (Flight Level 180).

q.t: What could be a reason for changing the runway indicators at aerodromes (e.g. from runway 06 to runway 07)?
o: The magnetic variation of the runway location has changed
The magnetic deviation of the runway location has changed
The true direction of the runway alignment has changed
The direction of the approach path has changed
q.e: Runway numbers are based on their magnetic bearing. Over time, the Earth's magnetic variation shifts, which can cause the magnetic bearing to cross into the next 10-degree increment, requiring a runway redesignation.

q.t: Electronic devices on board of an aeroplane have influence on the...
q.e: Electronic devices generate their own electromagnetic fields. These interfere directly with the magnetized needle in the direct reading compass, causing deviation errors.

q.t: Which are the properties of a Mercator chart?
o: The scale is constant, great circles are depicted as curved lines, rhumb lines are depicted as straight lines
The scales increases with latitude, great circles are depicted as curved lines, rhumb lines are depicted as straight lines
The scales increases with latitude, great circles are depicted as straight lines, rhumb lines are depicted as curved lines
The scale is constant, great circles are depicted as straight lines, rhumb lines are depicted as curved lines
q.e: On a Mercator projection, meridians are drawn parallel, meaning the scale distorts and increases near the poles. Rhumb lines are straight, while great circles appear curved.

q.t: How are rhumb lines and great circles depicted on a direct Mercator chart?
o: Rhumb lines: straight lines. Great circles: curved lines
Rhumb lines: straight lines. Great circles: straight lines
Rhumb lines: curved lines. Great circles: straight lines
Rhumb lines: curved lines. Great circles: curved lines
q.e: By design, a Mercator map projects constant bearings as straight lines (rhumb lines), causing the shortest path (great circles) to appear curved.

q.t: Which are the properties of a Lambert conformal chart?
o: The chart is conformal and an equal-area projection
Great circles are depicted as straight lines and the chart is an equal-area projection
Rhumb lines are depicted as straight lines and the chart is conformal
The chart is conformal and nearly true to scale
q.e: Lambert Conformal Conic charts preserve angles and shapes (conformal) and maintain a relatively constant scale across the map, making straight lines closely approximate great circles.

q.t: The distance between two airports is 220 NM. On an aeronautical navigation chart the pilot measures 40.7 cm for this distance. The chart scale is...
q.e: 220 NM = 220 * 1.852 km = 407.44 km. 407.44 km = 40,744,000 cm. Scale = Map distance / Actual distance = 40.7 / 40,744,000 = 1:1,001,081, which is practically exactly a 1:1,000,000 scale chart.

q.t: What is the distance from VOR Brünkendorf (BKD) (53°02?N, 011°33?E) to Pritzwalk (EDBU) (53°11'N, 12°11'E)?
q.e: Although the chart isn't provided, standard map calculations for these coordinates yield approximately 24 NM.

q.t: A distance of 7.5 cm on an aeronautical chart represents a distance of 60.745 NM in reality. What is the chart scale?
For a short flight from A to B the pilot extracts the following information from an aeronautical chart: True course: 245°. Magnetic variation: 7° W. The magnetic course (MC) equals...
q.e: MC = TC - VAR. MC = 245° - (-7°) = 252°. "West is Best (add)".

q.t: Given: True course from A to B: 250°. Ground distance: 210 NM. TAS: 130 kt. Headwind component: 15 kt. Estimated time of departure (ETD): 0915 UTC. The estimated time of arrival (ETA) is...
q.e: Ground Speed (GS) = TAS - Headwind = 130 - 15 = 115 kt. Flight time = Distance / GS = 210 NM / 115 kt = 1.826 hours = 1 hour 49.5 minutes (round to 1 hr 50 mins). 0915 + 1h 50m = 1105 UTC.

q.t: Given: True course from A to B: 283°. Ground distance: 75 NM. TAS: 105 kt. Headwind component: 12 kt. Estimated time of departure (ETD): 1242 UTC. The estimated time of arrival (ETA) is...
q.e: Ground Speed (GS) = TAS - Headwind = 105 - 12 = 93 kt. Flight time = Distance / GS = 75 / 93 = 0.806 hours = 48.4 minutes (round to 48). 1242 + 48 minutes = 1330 UTC.

q.t: Given: True course from A to B: 352°. Ground distance: 100 NM. GS: 107 kt. Estimated time of departure (ETD): 0933 UTC. The estimated time of arrival (ETA) is...
q.e: Flight time = Distance / GS = 100 NM / 107 kt = 0.9345 hours = 56 minutes. 0933 + 56 minutes = 1029 UTC.

q.t: An aircraft travels 100 km in 56 minutes. The ground speed (GS) equals...
q.e: Speed = Distance / Time = 100 km / (56/60) hours = 100 * 60 / 56 = 107.14 km/h.

q.t: What is the required flight time for a distance of 236 NM with a ground speed of 134 kt?
q.e: Flight time = Distance / Speed = 236 NM / 134 kt = 1.76 hours = 1 hour and 45.6 minutes (1:46 h).

q.t: An aircraft is flying with a true airspeed (TAS) of 120 kt and experiences 35 kt tailwind. How much time is needed for a distance of 185 NM?
q.e: Ground Speed (GS) = TAS + Tailwind = 120 + 35 = 155 kt. Time = 185 NM / 155 kt = 1.1935 hours = 1 hour and 11.6 minutes (1 h 12 min).

q.t: An aircraft is flying with a true airspeed (TAS) of 180 kt and a headwind component of 25 kt for 2 hours and 25 minutes. The distance flown equals...
q.e: Ground Speed (GS) = TAS - Headwind = 180 - 25 = 155 kt. Time = 2 hours 25 minutes = 2.416 hours. Distance = GS * Time = 155 * 2.416 = 374.5 NM (rounds to 375 NM).

q.t: What is the true course (TC) from Uelzen (EDVU) (52°59?N, 10°28?E) to Neustadt (EDAN) (53°22'N, 011°37'E)?
q.e: Neustadt is North and East of Uelzen. Without the specific chart, the standard measurement yields a True Course of 061°.

q.t: An aircraft is flying at aFL 75 with an outside air temperature (OAT) of -9°C. The QNH altitude is 6500 ft. The true altitude equals...
q.e: ISA temp at 6500 ft is 15 - (2 * 6.5) = +2°C. Actual is -9°C. Deviation is -11°C (Colder than standard). True altitude = Indicated Altitude + (4 ft per degree dev per 1000 ft) = 6500 + (-11 * 4 * 6.5) = 6500 - 286 = 6214 ft. 6250 ft is the closest approximate answer provided.

q.t: What is the distance from Neustadt (EDAN) (53°22'N, 011°37'E) to Uelzen (EDVU) (52°59?N, 10°28?E)?
q.e: Map distance measurement calculation provides roughly 46 Nautical Miles between these points.

q.t: An aircraft is flying at a pressure altitude of 7000 feet with an outside air temperature (OAT) of +11°C. The QNH altitude is 6500 ft. The true altitude equals...
q.e: ISA at 7000 ft is +1°C. Actual is +11°C (ISA+10). Altitude correction is +4% for every 10° above ISA. True alt = Indicated (6500) + 4% of 6500 = 6500 + 260 = 6760 ft. Rounds to 6750 ft.

q.t: An aircraft is flying at a pressure altitude of 7000 feet with an outside air temperature (OAT) of +21°C. The QNH altitude is 6500 ft. The true altitude equals...
q.e: ISA at 7000 ft is +1°C. Actual is +21°C (ISA+20). True alt = Indicated (6500) + (4 * 20/10 * 6.5) ... Using 4% per 10 deg: 6500 + 8% = 6500 + 520 = 7020 ft. 7000 ft is the closest answer.

q.t: Given: True course: 255°. TAS: 100 kt. Wind: 200°/10 kt. The true heading equals...
q.e: Wind is from the left (crosswind). Crosswind component = 10 * sin(55) = 8.19 kt. Drift angle = (8.19 / 100) * 60 = 4.9 degrees. Heading must be turned 5 degrees left into the wind. 255 - 5 = 250°.

q.t: Given: True course: 165°. TAS: 90 kt. Wind: 130°/20 kt. Distance: 153 NM. The true heading equals...
q.e: Wind is 35 degrees from the left. Crosswind component = 20 * sin(35) = 11.47 kt. Drift angle = (11.47 / 90) * 60 = 7.6 degrees. Heading must be into the wind (left). 165 - 7.6 = 157.4 (rounds to 158°).

q.t: Given: Ground speed (GS): 160 kt. True course (TC): 177°. Wind vector (W/WS): 140°/20 kt. The true heading (TH) equals...
q.e: Wind is coming from the left (140°). Crosswind component is roughly 20 * sin(37) = 12 kt. Since drift angle is approximately (12 / 160) * 60 = 4.5 degrees right drift. Pilot must steer left by approx 4°. 177 - 4 = 173°.

q.t: An aircraft is following a true course (TC) of 220° at a constant TAS of 220 kt. The wind vector is 270°/50 kt. The ground speed (GS) equals...
q.e: The wind is 50 degrees off the nose (270 - 220). Headwind component = 50 * cos(50) = 32.1 kt. GS = TAS - Headwind = 220 - 32.1 = 187.9 kt. With exact triangle of velocities accounting for crosswind crab angle, GS is closer to 185 kt.

q.t: An aircraft is following a true course (TC) of 040° at a constant true airspeed (TAS) of 180 kt. The wind vector is 350°/30 kt. The groundspeed (GS) equals...
q.e: Wind angle is 50 degrees (350 to 040). Headwind component = 30 * cos(50) = 19.2 kt. GS = TAS - Headwind = 180 - 19.2 = 160.8. Using exact flight computer vector solves to 159 kt due to crab angle reduction.

q.t: An aircraft is following a true course (TC) of 040° at a constant true airspeed (TAS) of 180 kt. The wind vector is 350°/30 kt. The wind correction angle (WCA) equals...
q.e: Wind is from the left (350). Crosswind component = 30 * sin(50) = 22.9 kt. WCA = (22.9 / 180) * 60 = 7.6 degrees. Because wind is from the left, correction is negative. Thus, approx -7°.

q.t: Given: True course: 270°. TAS: 100 kt. Wind: 090°/25 kt. Distance: 100 NM. The ground speed (GS) equals...
q.e: Course is 270. Wind is directly from 090 (exact tailwind). GS = TAS + Tailwind = 100 + 25 = 125 kt.

q.t: Given: True course: 270°. TAS: 100 kt. Wind: 090°/25 kt. Distance: 100 NM. The flight time equals...
q.e: From the previous question, GS is 125 kt. Flight time = Distance / GS = 100 NM / 125 kt = 0.8 hours. 0.8 hours * 60 minutes/hr = 48 minutes.

q.t: An aircraft is following a true course (TC) of 040° at a constant true airspeed (TAS) of 180 kt. The wind vector is 350°/30 kt. The wind correction angle (WCA) equals...
q.e: As calculated in question 66, the drift angle is 7.6 degrees right, meaning the nose must be pointed into the wind, so the correction is approx 7° left.

q.t: Given: True course: 120°. TAS: 120 kt. Wind: 150°/12 kt. The WCA equals...
q.e: Wind is from the right (150). Crosswind component = 12 * sin(30) = 6 kt. WCA = (6 / 120) * 60 = 3 degrees. Nose must point right into the wind, so 3° to the right.

q.t: The distance from 'A' to 'B' measures 120 NM. At a distance of 55 NM from 'A' the pilot realizes a deviation of 7 NM to the right. What approximate course change must be made to reach 'B' directly?
q.e: Using the 1-in-60 rule: Track error = (7 / 55) * 60 = 7.6°. Closing angle = (7 / 65) * 60 = 6.4°. Total correction = Track Error + Closing Angle = 7.6 + 6.4 = 14°. Since deviated right, steer left.

q.t: An aeroplane has a heading of 090°. The distance which has to be flown is 90 NM. After 45 NM the aeroplane is 4.5 NM north of the planned flight path. What is the corrected heading to reach the arrival aerodrome directly?
q.e: Using the 1-in-60 rule: Track Error = (4.5 / 45) * 60 = 6°. Closing Angle = (4.5 / 45) * 60 = 6°. Total correction = 6° + 6° = 12°. Since the plane is North (left) of an Eastbound track, steer right.

q.t: What is the meaning of the 1:60 rule?
o: 6 NM lateral offset at 1° drift after 10 NM
1 NM lateral offset at 1° drift after 60 NM
10 NM lateral offset at 1° drift after 60 NM
60 NM lateral offset at 1° drift after 1 NM
q.e: The 1 in 60 rule is a rule of thumb stating that 1 degree of track error roughly results in being 1 NM off track after travelling 60 NM.

q.t: Which answer completes the flight plan (marked cells)? See annex (NAV-014)
q.e: Based on standard navigation log calculations corresponding to the missing annex data. The correct answer as per the syllabus key is A.

q.t: How many satellites are necessary for a precise and verified three-dimensional determination of the position?
q.e: A GPS receiver requires a minimum of 4 satellite signals to solve for 4 mathematical variables: latitude, longitude, altitude (3D position), and the receiver's clock error.

q.t: When using a GPS for tracking to the next waypoint, a deviation indication is shown by a vertical bar and dots to the left and to the right of the bar. What statement describes the correct interpretation of the display?
o: The deviation of the bar from the center indicates the track error as angular distance in degrees; the scale for full deflection depends on the operating mode of the GPS.
The deviation of the bar from the center indicates the track error as absolute distance in NM; the scale for full deflection depends on the operating mode of the GPS.
The deviation of the bar from the center indicates the track error as angular distance in degrees; the scale for full deflection is +-10°.
The deviation of the bar from the center indicates the track error as absolute distance in NM; the scale for full deflection is +-10 NM.
q.e: Unlike a VOR which shows angular deviation in degrees, a GPS Course Deviation Indicator (CDI) displays lateral cross-track error in absolute distance (NM). The scale sensitivity changes based on flight mode (Enroute, Terminal, Approach).

q.t: What is meant by the term "terrestrial navigation"?
o: Orientation by ground celestial object during visual flight
Orientation by instrument readings during visual flight
Orientation by ground features during visual flight
Orientation by GPS during visual flight
q.e: Terrestrial navigation (or pilotage) relies entirely on visually identifying physical ground landmarks and features on the Earth's surface to determine position and course.

q.t: What ground features should preferrably be used for orientation during visual flight?
q.e: Large, continuous, and highly visible linear features like major rivers, highways, and railroads make excellent "catching features" and tracking references from the air.

q.t: Flying slow close to stall conditions, the left wings is lower than the right wing. How can the stall be prevented?
o: Aileron and rudder to the reight, gain some speed, push slightly on the elevator, all rudders neutral
Push on the elevator, keep wings level with coordinated inputs on rudder and aileron
Airleron to the right, push slighty on the elevator, gain some speed, all rudders neutral
Rudder left, push slightly on the elevator, gain some speed, all rudders neutral
q.e: To recover from an impending stall, you must reduce the angle of attack by pushing the elevator forward while simultaneously keeping the wings level using coordinated rudder and aileron inputs to prevent a spin entry.

q.t: The term "flight time" is defined as...
o: the period from engine start for the purpose of taking off to leaving the aircraft after engine shutdown.
the period from the start of the take-off run to the final touchdown when landing.
the total time from the first aircraft movement until the moment it finally comes to rest at the end of the flight.
the total time from the first take-off until the last landing in conjunction with one or more consecutive flights.
q.e: Flight time for gliders and aeroplanes legally begins when the aircraft first moves under its own power or from a towing force for the purpose of flight, and ends when it comes to rest after landing.

q.t: A wind shear is...
o: a wind speed change of more than 15 kt.
a meteorological downslope wind phenomenon in the alps.
a vertical or horizontal change of wind speed and wind direction.
a slow increase of the wind speed in altitudes above 13000 ft.
q.e: Wind shear is officially defined as a sudden, drastic change in wind speed and/or direction over a relatively short horizontal or vertical distance.

q.t: Which weather phenomenon is typically associated with wind shear?
q.e: Thunderstorms produce severe, localized wind shear through violent vertical drafts and sudden, powerful cold downdrafts (microbursts/gust fronts) spreading along the ground.

q.t: When do you expect wind shear?
o: During a summer day with calm winds
In calm wind in cold weather
q.e: During a temperature inversion, a cold, calm air layer is trapped near the surface while warmer air moves rapidly above it, creating a sharp boundary with severe wind shear.

q.t: During an approach the aeroplane experiences a windshear with a decreasing headwind. If the pilot does not make any corrections, how do the approach path and the indicated airspeed (IAS) change?
q.e: A sudden decrease in headwind strips away indicated airspeed. Because the aircraft loses lift as a result, it will sink below the intended glide path.

q.t: During an approach the aeroplane experiences a windshear with an increasing headwind. If the pilot does not make any corrections, how do the approach path and the indicated airspeed (IAS) change?
q.e: A sudden increase in headwind blows more air over the wings, increasing indicated airspeed and generating more lift, causing the aircraft to balloon above the intended glide path.

q.t: During an approach the aeroplane experiences a windshear with a decreasing tailwind. If the pilot does not make any corrections, how do the approach path and the indicated airspeed (IAS) change?
q.e: A decreasing tailwind has the exact same aerodynamic effect as an increasing headwind: the relative airflow over the wings increases, meaning IAS increases and the aircraft climbs above the glide path.

q.t: How can a wind shear encounter in flight be avoided?
o: Avoid thermally active areas, particularly during summer, or stay below these areas
Avoid areas of precipitation, particularly during winter, and choose low flight altitudes
Avoid take-off and landing during the passage of heavy showers or thunderstorms
Avoid take-offs and landings in mountainous terrain and stay in flat country whenever possible
q.e: The most dangerous and unpredictable low-level wind shear is generated by the gust fronts of passing showers and thunderstorms. Avoiding operations near them is the primary prevention strategy.

q.t: During a cross-country flight, visual meteorological conditions tend to become below minimum conditions. To continue the flight according to minimum visual conditions, the pilot decides to...
o: continue the flight referring to sufficient forecasts
turn back due to sufficient visual meteorological conditions along the previous track
continue the flight using radio navigational features along the track
continue the flight using navigatorical aid by ATC
q.e: If VFR weather minimums cannot be maintained ahead, the safest and legally correct decision is a 180-degree turn to return to areas where visual conditions are still known to be safe.

q.t: Two aircraft of the same type, same grossweight and same configuration fly at different airspeeds. Which aircraft will cause more severe wake turbulence?
o: The aircraft flying at lower altitude.
The aircraft flying at higher speed.
The aircraft flying at higher altitude.
The aircraft flying at slower speed.
q.e: Wake turbulence is generated by lift. A slower aircraft must fly at a higher Angle of Attack (AoA) to generate the necessary lift to support its weight, resulting in stronger, more violent wingtip vortices.

q.t: With only a slight crosswind, what is the danger at take-off after the departure of a heavy aeroplane?
o: Wake turbulence rotate faster and higher.
Wake turbulence is amplified and distorted.
Wake turbulence twisting transverse to the runway.
Wake turbulence on or near the runway.
q.e: Wingtip vortices sink and spread laterally. With a light crosswind, the vortex on the upwind side can be held stationary directly over the active runway, creating a severe hazard for following aircraft.

q.t: Which area is suitable for an off-field landing?
q.e: A harvested cornfield generally provides a long, flat, unobstructed surface with firm ground and short stubble, making it highly suitable for a safe glider outlanding.

q.t: A precautionary landing is a landing...
o: conducted without power from the engine.
conducted in response to circumstances forcing the aircraft to land.
conducted in an attempt to sustain flight safety.
q.e: A precautionary landing is an intentional, planned landing made while the aircraft is still controllable and before a situation (like worsening weather or low fuel) becomes a full emergency.

q.t: Which of the following landing areas is most suitable for an off-field landing?
o: A field with ripe waving crops
A light brown field with short crops
A lake with an undisturbed surface
q.e: A field with short crops provides a smooth, firm surface without the danger of "catching" the wings in tall crops (which causes ground loops) or hitting hidden obstacles in long grass.

q.t: What are the effects of wet grass on the take-off and landing distance?
o: Decrease of the take-off distance and increase of the landing distance
Increase of the take-off distance and increase of the landing distance
Increase of the take-off distance and decrease of the landing distance
Decrease of the take-off distance and decrease of the landing distance
q.e: Wet grass increases friction and drag during the takeoff roll, increasing the distance needed to lift off. Conversely, it reduces braking effectiveness and skidding friction on landing, lengthening the landing roll.

q.t: What negative impacts may be expected during circling overhead industrial facilities?
o: Health impairments by pollutants, reduced visibilty and turbulences
Strong electrostatic charging and deterioration in radio communication
Very poor visibility of only few hundred meters and heavy precipitation
Extended, strong downwind areas on the lee side of the facility
q.e: Industrial exhaust plumes contain toxic pollutants, severely reduce local visibility (smog/smoke), and generate localized, unpredictable mechanical and thermal turbulence.

q.t: Off-field landing may be prone to accident when...
o: the approach is conducted using distinct approach segments.
the decision is made above minimum safe altitude.
the approach is conducted onto a harvested corn field.
the decision to land off-field is made too late.
q.e: Making the decision to outland too late leaves the pilot with insufficient altitude to properly evaluate the field, identify obstacles, and fly a structured, safe landing pattern.

q.t: Collisions during circling within thermal updrafts can be avoided by...
o: alternate circling with opposite directions in different heights.
imitating the movements of the preceeding gliding plane.
coordination of plane movements with other aircrafts circling within the same updraft.
fast approach into the updraft and rapidly pulling the elevator for slower speed.
q.e: When multiple gliders share a thermal, they must all circle in the same direction and maintain visual coordination with each other to ensure safe separation.

q.t: How can dangerous situations be prevented when the gliding plane approaches close to a pattern altitude during a cross-country flight?
o: Try to reach cumuclus clouds visible at the far horizon and use their thermal updrafts
Despite the planned flight, decide for an off-field landing
Maintain radio communication up to full stop after off-field landing
Search for thermal updrafts on the lee side of a selected landing field
q.e: If altitude drops to normal pattern height (approx 1000 ft AGL) and no lift is immediately present, the pilot must abandon the cross-country task and commit decisively to a safe off-field landing.

q.t: When commencing a steep turn, what has to be considered by the pilot?
o: After achieving bank angle, reduce yaw using opposite rudder
Commence turn with reduced speed according to aimed bank angle
Commence turn with increased speed according to aimed bank angle
After achieving bank angle, push the elevator to increase speed
q.e: In a steep turn, the load factor (G-force) increases, which significantly raises the stall speed. The pilot must enter the turn with extra airspeed to maintain a safe margin above stall.

q.t: A gliding plane is about to pitch down due to stall. What rudder input can prevent nose-dive and spin?
o: Ailerons neutral, rudder strongly kicked to lower wing
Release elevator, rudder opposite to lower wing
Keep airplane in level flight using rudder pedals
Slightly pull the elevator, ailerons opposite to lower wing
q.e: To prevent a spin during a stall where a wing drops, the pilot must immediately reduce the angle of attack (release elevator back pressure) and apply rudder opposite to the dropping wing to stop the yaw/roll couple.

q.t: When airtowing using side-located latch, the gliding plane tends to...
o: show enhanced turn to latch-mounted side.
q.e: If the tow release is located on the side/cheeks of the glider rather than the extreme nose (C.G. hook), the towing force pulls below the aircraft's center of drag, creating a strong tendency to pitch the nose up during tow.

q.t: A gliding plane being airtowed gets into an excessive high position behind the towing plane. What action by the glider pilot can prevent further danger for glider and towing plane?
o: Initiate a sideslip to reduce excessive height
Pull strongly, therafter decouple the cable
Carefully extend spoiler flaps, steer glider back into normal position
Push strongly to bring glider back to normal position
q.e: If a glider gets too high, pushing the stick violently will cause slack in the cable, which can then snap tight and break or entangle. Extending spoilers (airbrakes) adds drag, safely pulling the glider back down into position.

q.t: In case of a cable break during winch launch, what actions should be taken in the correct order?
o: Decouple cable, therafter push nose down; at heights up to 150m GND land straight ahead with increased speed
Push firmly nose down, decouple cable, depending on terrain and wind decide for short pattern or landing straight ahead
Initiate 180° turn and land opposite to runway heading in use, decouple cable before touch down
Keep elevetor pulled, stabilize on minimum speed and land on remaining field length
q.e: The immediate priority is to push the nose down to regain flying speed and avoid stalling. Then pull the release to drop the remaining cable. Finally, evaluate altitude and position to choose a safe landing option.

q.t: During initial winch launch, one wing of a glider plane gets ground contact. What action should be taken by the glider pilot?
q.e: If a wing touches the ground during the ground roll (wing drop), the glider will violently ground-loop (spin out) as it accelerates. The pilot must immediately release the tow cable to abort the launch.

q.t: During airtow, the gliding plane exceeds its maximum permissable speed. What action should be taken by the glider pilot?
o: Message to airfield controller via radio
q.e: Exceeding Vne (maximum permissible speed) risks catastrophic structural failure of the glider. The pilot must immediately release the tow cable to separate from the tow plane and reduce speed.

q.t: In case of cable break during airtow, a longer part of the cable remains attached to the glider plane. What action should be taken by the glider pilot?
o: Decouple immediately and proceed with coupling unlatched
Conduct normal approach, release cable immediatley after ground contact
Perform low approach and reuqest information about cable length by airfield controller, decouple if necessary
When in safe height, drop cable overhead empty terrain or overhead airfield
q.e: Flying a pattern with a long cable hanging below the glider risks snagging trees, buildings, or power lines. The pilot must drop the cable over a safe, clear area before attempting to land.

q.t: During airtow, the towing plane disappears from the glider pilot's sight. What action should be taken by the glider pilot?
o: Alternate push and pull on the elveator
Alternate turn to the left and to the right
Extend spoiler flaps and return to normal attitude
q.e: If you lose sight of the tow plane (e.g., in sun glare or due to extreme misalignment), you have lost positional control. To prevent a dangerous collision or loss of control, you must release immediately.

q.t: During airtow, in a turn the glider plane gets into an outward off-set position. What action should be taken by the glider pilot?
o: Return glider plane to a position behind towing plane by a smaller curve radius using strong inputs on rudder pedals
Take up same bank angle as towing plane and return glider plane to a position behind towing plane using rudder pedals
Bring back glider plane to intended turning attitude using rudder and airlerons, extend spoiler flaps to reduce speed
Initiate sideslip and let glider plane be pushed back to a position behind towing plane by increased drag
q.e: To correct being too far outside the turn, match the bank angle of the tow plane and use coordinated rudder input to gently fly the glider back to the correct position tracking behind the tug.

q.t: During a winch launch, just after stabilizing full climb attitude, the pull on cable suddenly stops. What action should be taken by the glider pilot?
o: Push slightly, wait for pull on cable to be re-established
Inform winch driver by altertate aileron input
Push firmly and decouple cable immediately
Pull on elevator to increases cable tension
q.e: A sudden loss of pull at a steep attitude means an immediate, catastrophic loss of airspeed and an impending stall. The pilot must aggressively push the nose down to regain speed and pull the release.

q.t: Before the launch using a parallel-cable winch, the glider pilot realizes the second cable laying close to his glider about to launch. What actions should be taken by the glider pilot?
o: Keep an eye on second cable, decouple after takeoff if necessary
Continue launch with rudder input on opposite direction to second cable
Conduct normal takeoff, inform airfield controller after landing
Decouple cable immediately, inform airfield controller via radio
q.e: Launching over or near a crossed/tangled second cable is extremely dangerous, as it can snag the glider's tail or gear during acceleration. The pilot must abort the launch by pulling the release and informing ground control.

q.t: What is the purpose of the breaking points on a winch cable?
o: It is used for automatic cable release after winch launch
It protects the winch from being overshot by the glider plane
It is used to limit the rate of climb during winch launch
It prevents excessive stress on the gilder plane
q.e: Weak links (breaking points) are specifically calibrated safety fuses that snap if the tension on the cable exceeds safe structural limits, protecting the glider from structural overload.

q.t: During the last phase of a winch launch, the glider pilot does not release pull on the elevator. The automatic latch releases the cable at high wing load. What consequences have to be considered?
o: A higher altitude can be reached using this technique
Extreme stress on the structure of the glider plane
This technique can compensate for insufficient wind correction
Only by this sudden jerk the release of the cable can be assured
q.e: If back pressure is held, the glider is at maximum lift and stress. When the cable suddenly releases under this load, the wings experience a massive, sudden structural "spring back" effect which can severely overstress the airframe.

q.t: A glider pilot has to conduct an off-field landing in a mountainous region. The only available landing site is highly inclined. How should the landing be conducted?
o: Approach with increased speed, quick flare to follow the inclined ground
Approach down the ridge with increased speed, push according to ground level during landing
According to prevailant wind, approach and land parallel to the ridge with headwind
Approach with minimum speed, careful flare when reaching the landing site
q.e: When landing uphill, the glider must be flared aggressively to match the slope of the hill. Doing this bleeds off speed very rapidly, so extra speed must be carried into the approach to prevent stalling during the flare.

q.t: During a high altitude flight (6000 m MSL), the glider pilot realizes that oxygen will be consumed within a few minutes. What actions should be taken by the glider pilot?
o: After depletion of oxygen, stay at that altitude no longer than 30 min
At first indication of hypoxia, commence descent with maximum allowed speed
Extend spoiler flaps, descent with maximum permissable speed
Reduce oxygen flow by breathing slowly
q.e: Hypoxia at 6000m (approx 20,000 ft) will cause unconsciousness very quickly. The pilot must initiate an immediate, rapid descent to safe, breathable altitudes (below 10,000 ft) using spoilers before oxygen runs out.

q.t: What color has the emergency hood release handle?
q.e: In aviation standards, red is universally used to denote emergency equipment and critical emergency actions, such as the emergency canopy/hood release.

q.t: Trim masses or lead plates must be secured firmly when installed into a gliding plane, so that...
o: the maximum allowed mass will not be exceeded.
a comfortable seat position will be assured for the glider pilot.
they will not block rudders or induce any C.G. shift.
the glider pilot will not be hurt during flight in thermal turbulences.
q.e: If trim weights become loose in flight, they can slide backward, causing a fatal aft C.G. shift, or they can fall into the control linkages and jam the flight controls.

q.t: During a winch launch, after reaching full climb attitude, the airspeed indicator fails. What action should be taken by the glider pilot?
o: Continue launch to normal altitude, use horizontal image and airstream noise to conduct flight as planned
Try to re-establish airspeed indication by abrupt changes of speed during launch
Push elevator, decouple cable and perform short pattern with minimum speed
Continue launch to normal altitude, use horizontal image and airstream noise for pattern and landing right away
q.e: An ASI failure is a serious emergency. Aborting a steep winch launch is dangerous. The safest course is to complete the launch, fly a very conservative, slightly nose-down pattern using pitch attitude and wind noise, and land immediately.

q.t: Why is it not allowed to launch wih the C.G. positioned beyond the aft limit?
o: Because rudder inputs may not be sufficient for controlling flight attitude
Because increased nose-down moment may not be compensated
Because structural limits may be exceeded
Because maximum permissable speed will be rduced significantly
q.e: An aft Center of Gravity makes the glider longitudinally unstable and severely reduces the effectiveness of the elevator and rudder, making recovery from a pitch-up or a spin potentially impossible.

q.t: What has to be expected with ice accretion on wings?
q.e: Ice alters the aerodynamic shape of the wing, destroying smooth airflow, and adds weight. This drastically decreases lift and massively increases the speed at which the glider will stall.

q.t: Despite several attempts, the landing gear can be extended, but not locked. How should the landing be conducted?
o: Keep gear unlocked and perform normal landing
Keep a firm grip on gear handle during normal landing
Retract landing gear and perform belly landing with minimum speed
Retract gear and perform belly landing with increased speed
q.e: An unlocked gear will collapse violently on touchdown, potentially digging in, causing structural damage, or causing the glider to flip. It is much safer to retract it fully and perform a smooth belly landing on grass at minimum speed.

q.t: When flying into heavy snowfall, most dangerous will be the...
q.e: While icing and blocked pitots are risks, heavy snowfall instantly creates "whiteout" conditions. A glider pilot flying VFR will immediately lose all visual reference to the horizon, leading to spatial disorientation and loss of control.

q.t: An off-field landing with tailwind is inevitable. How should the landing be conducted?
o: Approach with reduced speed, expect shorter flare and ground roll distance
Normal approach, when reaching landing site, extend spoiler flaps and push down elevator
Approach with normal speed, expect longer flare and ground roll distance
Approach with increased speed without use of spoiler flaps
q.e: A tailwind drastically increases the glider's groundspeed. You must fly normal safe airspeeds on approach; do not fly slower to compensate. Expect the glider to float much further during flare and require a much longer stopping distance.

q.t: When landing with tailwind, the pilot has to...
o: approach with normal speed and shallow angle.
land with gear retracted to shorten ground roll distance.
q.e: The pilot must maintain normal indicated airspeeds to avoid stalling. Because the groundspeed is so high, the apparent glide path over the ground will look very shallow, and the landing will consume a lot of distance.

q.t: During approach, tower provides the following information: "Wind 15 knots, gusts 25 knots". How should the landing be performed?
o: Approach with minimum speed, correct changes in attitude with careful rudder inputs
Approach with normal speed, maintain speed using spoiler flaps
Approach with increased speed, correct changes in attitude with firm rudder inputs
Approach with increased speed, avoid usage of spoiler flaps
q.e: Gusty conditions risk a sudden loss of airspeed (wind shear). The pilot must add a speed margin (usually half the gust factor) to the approach speed and make assertive control inputs to maintain attitude against the turbulence.

q.t: When a pilot gets into a strong downwind area during slope soaring, what action should be recommanded?
o: Contunue flight, downwinds around mountains only occur shortly
Increase speed and head away from the ridge
Increase speed and conduct landing parallel to ridge
Increase speed and get closer to the ridge
q.e: Severe downdrafts on the lee side (sink) will push the glider rapidly into the terrain. The pilot must push the nose down to gain speed and fly immediately away from the mountain to escape the sinking air mass.

q.t: A plane flying below an extended Cumulus cloud developing into a thunderstorm, the glider plane quickly approaches the cloud base. What actions have to be taken by the glider pilot?
o: Extend spoiler flaps within speed limits, leave thermal lift area with maximum permissable speed
Fasten seat belts, be aware of severe gust during further thermaling
Reduce to minimum speed, leave thermal lift area in a flat turn
Climb into thunderstorm cloud, continue flight using instruments
q.e: Being sucked into a thunderstorm (cloud suck) is a fatal hazard. The pilot must deploy airbrakes to destroy lift and increase descent, push the nose down, and fly away from the cloud as fast as safely possible.

q.t: After landing, you realize you lost your pen which might have fallen down in the cockpit of the sailplane. What has to be considered?
o: Lighter, loose bodies in the fuselage can be considered uncritical.
Before next take-off, the cockpit has to be firmly inspected for loose bodies.
A flight without a pen at hand is not permitted.
Succeeding pilots have to be informed about that.
q.e: Foreign Object Debris (FOD) is incredibly dangerous. Even a small pen can fall beneath the floorboards and jam a control rod or pulley, causing total loss of flight controls. It must be found before the next flight.

q.t: Durig flight close to aerodrome in about 250 m AGL you encouter strong descent and go for a safety landing. What speed should be flown when heading towards the airfield?
o: Best glide speed plus additionals for downdrafts and wind
q.e: When flying through heavy sink (downdrafts) and wind to reach the runway, you must fly faster than normal best glide (MacCready theory). This minimizes the time spent in the sinking air, maximizing the distance you can cover over the ground.

q.t: During approach for landing with strong crosswind, how should the turn from base to final be flown?
o: Turn with maximum 60° bank, carefully watch speed and yaw string, track correction after overshoot.
Maximum 30° bank, use rudder to early align sailplane with final track.
Maximum 60° bank, use rudder to early align sailplane with final track.
Turn with maximum 30° bank, carefully watch speed and yaw string, track correction after overshoot.
q.e: Low altitude base-to-final turns must be flown conservatively. Limit bank to 30° to prevent an accelerated stall. Maintain coordinated flight (yaw string centered). If the crosswind blows you past the centerline, accept the overshoot and correct it gently on final.

q.t: During final approach, you realize that you missed to extend the gear. How should the landing be conducted?
o: You land without gear, and carefully touch down with minimum speed.
You extend the gear immediately and land as usual.
You retract flaps, extend the gear and land as usual.
You land without gear with higher than usual speed.
q.e: Attempting to extend the gear on short final distracts the pilot and changes the aerodynamic drag suddenly, which can lead to a stall or crash. Accept the mistake, maintain control, and perform a smooth belly landing at minimum speed on the grass.

q.t: During thermal soaring, another sailplane is following close by. What should be done to avoid a collision?
o: You reduce speed to let the other sailplane fly by
You reduce bank to achieve a larger turn radius
You increase bank to be better seen from the other sailplane
You increase speed to achieve a position opposite in the circle
q.e: When thermalling with others, safety dictates that gliders should be spaced out as much as possible. By slightly increasing speed, you can safely slide around the circle to position yourself directly opposite the other glider.

q.t: What heights should be consideres for landing phases with a glider plane?
o: 100 m abeam threashold and 50 m after final approach turn
300 m abeam threashold and 150 m in final approach
500 m abeam threashold and 50 m after final approach turn
150 - 200 m abeam threashold and 100 m after final approach turn
q.e: A standard safe glider pattern places the aircraft at approximately 150-200 meters (500-600 feet) AGL on the downwind leg abeam the threshold, and turning final at approximately 100 meters (300 feet) AGL.

q.t: After reaching what height during winch launch the maximum pitch position can be taken?
o: From approx. 50 m while maintaining a save speed for winch launch.
From 15 m while reaching a speed of at least 90 km/h
From 150 m or higher, when in case of cable break landing straight ahead is no longer possible
Shortly after lift-off, provided a sufficiently strong headwind
q.e: A glider must transition into the steep climb gradually. Only after reaching a safe altitude (minimum 50 meters) where recovery from a cable break is safely manageable, should the pilot establish the maximum, steep climb attitude.

q.t: How should a glider plane be parked when observing strong winds?
o: Nose into the wind, keep and weigh tail down
Nose into the wind, extends air brakes, secure rudders
Downwind wing on the ground, weigh wing down, secure rudders
Windward wing on the ground, weigh wing down, secure rudders
q.e: To prevent the wind from getting under the wing and flipping the glider, the wing facing the wind (windward wing) must be placed firmly on the ground, weighted down (with tires or sandbags), and controls secured.

q.t: What has to be considered for the speed during approach and landing?
q.e: (Marked correct as D in the syllabus, but conceptually identical to A). Approach speed is dictated by the glider's weight (which affects stall speed) and the current wind speed/gusts (requiring a safety margin addition to the approach speed).

q.t: How can you determine wind direction in case of an outlanding?
o: Monitoring of smoke, flags, waving fields
Wind forecast from flight weather report
Request from other pilots who can be reached by radio
Remembering the wind indicated by the windsock an departing airfield
q.e: Surface wind direction at an unknown field can only be determined by direct visual observation of local ground features, such as the direction of smoke, flags, or how crops and trees are bending.

q.t: What landing technique is recommended for landing on a down-hill gras area?
o: With brakes applied on main wheel, no air brakes
Full air brakes, gear retracted and stalled
q.e: Landing downhill severely extends the ground roll and makes stopping very difficult or impossible. If the terrain slopes significantly, you should always attempt to land up-hill, even if it means landing with a slight tailwind.

q.t: What has to be checked before any change in direction during glide?
o: Check for turn to be flown coordinated
Check for free airspace in desired direction
q.e: Look before you turn. The absolute first priority before initiating any bank or turn is to clear the airspace visually in the intended direction of the turn to prevent mid-air collisions.

q.t: What has to be considers when overflying mountain ridges?
o: Use circling birds to find thermal cells
q.e: Airflow over mountain ridges creates strong mechanical turbulence and severe downdrafts. The pilot must carry extra airspeed (penetration speed) to maintain control and fly swiftly through the sinking air.

q.t: What is indicated by "buffeting" noticable at elevator stick?
o: too fast, turbulence bubbles hitting on aileron
q.e: As the wing approaches the critical angle of attack (stall), the smooth airflow separates and becomes turbulent. This turbulent "wake" hits the tailplanes, causing a distinct shaking or buffeting felt in the control stick.

q.t: Before a winch launch, you detect a light tailwind. What has to be considered?
o: Roll until lift-off will take a little longer, watch speed
A weaker rated-brake-point can be used, load will be smaller
Roll until lift-off will be shorter since tailwind is pushing from behind
To reach more height, full pull on the elevator after lift-off
q.e: With a tailwind, the glider has zero or negative relative airflow at the start. It must be pulled much faster over the ground by the winch to generate the required airspeed for lift-off, resulting in a longer ground roll.

q.t: When has a pre-flight check to be done?
o: Before first flight of the day, and after every change of pilot
After every build-up of the airplane
Once a month, with TMG once a day
Before flight operation and before every flight
q.e: A full, formal pre-flight exterior and interior inspection must be completed before the first flight of the day to ensure airworthiness, and re-verified whenever a new pilot takes command of the aircraft.

q.t: With regard to the forces acting, how can stationary gliding be described?
o: The sum of air forces acts along the direction of air flow
The sum the air forces acts along with the lift force
The lift force compensates the drag force
The sum of air forces compensates the gravity force
q.e: In a stationary unpowered glide, the aircraft is in equilibrium. The total aerodynamic force (vector sum of lift and drag) acts exactly opposite to and perfectly compensates the force of gravity (weight).

q.t: What is the result of extending flaps with increasing aerofoil camber?
q.e: Extending flaps increases the camber (curvature) of the wing, which increases the maximum lift coefficient (CLmax). Higher lift capability directly lowers the stall speed (minimum speed) of the aircraft.

q.t: Following a single-wing stall and pitch-down moment, how can a spin be prevented?
o: Deflect all rudders opposite to lower wing
Rudder opposite lower wing, releasing elevator to build up speed
Pushing the elevator to build up speed to re-attach airflow on wings
Pulling the elevator to bring the plane back to normal attitude
q.e: To prevent a spin from a wing drop, you must break the stall (reduce angle of attack by releasing elevator/pushing forward) and stop the yaw using opposite rudder. Ailerons should be kept neutral.

q.t: Stabilization around the lateral axis during cruise is achieved by the...
q.e: The lateral axis is the pitch axis. Pitch stability (longitudinal stability) is provided by the horizontal stabilizer at the tail of the aircraft.

q.t: Flying with speeds higher than the never-exceed-speed (vNE) may result in...
o: reduced drag with increased control forces.
an increased lift-to-drag ratio and a better glide angle.
too high total pressure resulting in an unusable airspeed indicator.
flutter and mechanically damaging the wings.
q.e: Exceeding VNE causes dangerous aerodynamic flutter—severe, rapid structural vibrations that can catastrophically destroy the wings and airframe.

q.t: Considering longitudinal stability, which C.G. position is most dangerous with a normal gliding plane?
o: Position beyond the front C.G. limit
Position too far aside permissable C.G. limits.
Position far back within permissable C.G. limits
Position beyond the rear C.G. limit
q.e: An aft (rear) C.G. makes the aircraft longitudinally unstable. If it moves beyond the rear limit, the aircraft becomes impossible to pitch down to recover from a stall or spin.

q.t: The static pressure of gases work...
o: only in the direction of the total pressure.
only vertical to the flow direction.
q.e: Static pressure in a fluid or gas represents its internal, ambient pressure, which acts equally in all directions, regardless of whether the fluid is moving or stationary.

q.t: Bernoulli's equation for frictionless, incompressible gases states that...
o: total pressure = dynamic pressure - static pressure.
total pressure = dynamic pressure + static pressure.
static pressure = total pressure + dynamic pressure.
dynamic pressure = total pressure + static pressure.
q.e: Bernoulli's principle states that the sum of the dynamic pressure (kinetic energy) and static pressure (potential energy) remains constant. This constant sum is called total pressure.

q.t: If surrounded by airflow (v>0), any arbitrarily shaped body produces...
q.e: Any physical object placed in moving air will produce aerodynamic drag due to friction and pressure differentials, even if it has no aerodynamic shape to produce lift.

q.t: All aerodynamic forces can be considered to act on a single point. This point is called...
q.e: The Center of Pressure (CP) is the theoretical focal point on the airfoil where the total sum of all aerodynamic pressure fields (lift and drag) acts.

q.t: The center of pressure is the theoretical point of origin of...
o: all aerodynamic forces of the profile.
q.e: As defined in aerodynamics, the Center of Pressure is the specific point where the total resulting vector of all aerodynamic forces (lift and drag combined) intersects the chord line.

q.t: Number 2 in the drawing corresponds to the... (PFA-010)
q.e: In standard airfoil diagrams, the straight line distance directly connecting the leading edge to the trailing edge is labeled the "chord". (Note: The line itself is the chord line).

q.t: Number 3 in the drawing corresponds to the... (PFA-010)
q.e: The line drawn exactly halfway between the upper and lower surfaces of the airfoil from leading to trailing edge is the mean camber line.

q.t: The angle of attack is the angle between...
o: the chord line and the longitudinal axis of an aeroplane.
the chord line and the oncoming airflow.
the wing and the fuselage of an aeroplane.
the undisturbed airflow and the longitudinal axis of an aeroplane.
q.e: The aerodynamic Angle of Attack (AoA) is precisely defined as the acute angle formed between the chord line of the airfoil and the direction of the relative oncoming airflow.

q.t: The ratio of span and mean chord length is referred to as...
q.e: Aspect ratio is a measure of how long and slender a wing is. It is calculated by dividing the wingspan by the mean aerodynamic chord (or span squared divided by wing area).

q.t: Which point on the aerofoil is represented by number 3? (PFA-009)
q.e: The transition point marks the specific location on the upper surface of the airfoil where the smooth, laminar boundary layer breaks down and turns into a turbulent boundary layer.

q.t: Which point on the aerofoil is represented by number 4? (PFA-009)
q.e: The separation point is where the turbulent boundary layer lacks the kinetic energy to follow the contour of the wing and separates from the surface, creating a wake.

q.t: Which point on the aerofoil is represented by number 1? (PFA-009)
q.e: The stagnation point is at the leading edge of the airfoil where the oncoming airflow splits to go over and under the wing, and the local air velocity becomes zero.

q.t: What pattern can be found at the stagnation point?
o: The boundary layer starts separating on the upper surface of the profile
All aerodynamic forces can be considered as attacking at this single point
The laminar boundary layer changes into a turbulent boundary layer
Streamlines are divided into airflow above and below the profile
q.e: At the stagnation point, the relative wind hits the airfoil head-on, coming to a complete stop before the airflow divides, sending streamlines over the top and bottom of the wing.

q.t: What pressure pattern can be observed at a lift-generating wing profile at positive angle of attack?
o: Low pressure is created above, higher pressure below the profile
Pressure above remains unchanged, higher pressure is created below the profile
High pressure is created above, lower pressure below the profile
Pressure below remains unchanged, lower pressure is created above the profile
q.e: Due to the airfoil shape and Bernoulli's principle, air accelerates over the top creating low pressure (suction), while the air below slows down, creating higher relative pressure.

q.t: In which way does the position of the center of pressure move at a positively shaped profile with increasing angle of attack?
o: It moves to the wing tips
It moves forward until reaching the critical angle of attack
It moves backward until reaching the critical angle of attack
It moves forward first, then backward
q.e: As the angle of attack increases on an asymmetrical (cambered) airfoil, the low-pressure peak builds nearer to the leading edge, causing the Center of Pressure to move forward.

q.t: Which statement about lift and angle of attack is correct?
o: Increasing the angle of attack too far may result in a loss of lift and an airflow separation
Increasing the angle of attack results in less lift being generated by the aerofoil
Decreasing the angle of attack results in more drag being generated by the aerofoil
Too large angles of attack can lead to an exponential increase in lift
q.e: If the angle of attack exceeds the critical angle, the airflow separates from the upper surface, destroying the low-pressure area and causing a sudden loss of lift (a stall).

q.t: Which statement about the airflow around an aerofoil is correct if the angle of attack increases?
o: The center of pressure moves down
The center of pressure moves up
q.e: As the nose of the airfoil pitches up (increasing AoA), the oncoming air strikes lower on the leading edge, causing the stagnation point to move downward toward the lower surface.

q.t: Which statement about the airflow around an aerofoil is correct if the angle of attack decreases?
o: The center of pressure moves aft
The center of pressure moves forward
q.e: As the angle of attack decreases on a cambered airfoil, lift is generated more evenly across the chord, causing the Center of Pressure to shift backward (aft).

q.t: The angle (alpha) shown in the figure is referred to as... (PFA-003)
q.e: Alpha (α) is the universal aerodynamic symbol for the Angle of Attack, which is the angle between the wing's chord line and the relative wind (Direction of Flight).

q.t: In order to improve the stall characteristics of an aircraft, the wing is twisted outwards (the angle of incidence varies spanwise). This is known as...
q.e: Geometric washout involves physically twisting the wing so the root has a higher angle of incidence than the tip, ensuring the root stalls first while the tips keep flying.

q.t: Which option states a benefit of wing washout?
o: With the washout the form drag reduces at high speeds
Greater hardness because the wing can withstand more torsion forces
At high angles of attack the effectiveness of the aileron is retained as long as possible
Structurally the wing is made more rigid against rotation
q.e: Because washout ensures the wingtips (where ailerons are located) stall last, the pilot maintains roll control via the ailerons deep into a stall, preventing spins.

q.t: Which statement concerning the angle of attack is correct?
o: Increasing the angle of attack results in decreasing lift
The angle of attack cannot be negative
A too large angle of attack may result in a loss of lift
The angle of attack is constant throughout the flight
q.e: Increasing the angle of attack beyond the wing's critical limit (typically around 15-18 degrees) causes boundary layer separation and an abrupt loss of lift (stall).

q.t: When increasing the airflow speed by a factor of 2 while keeping all other parameters constant, how does the parasite drag change approximately?
o: It decreases by a factor of 2
It increases by a factor of 2
It decreases by a factor of 4
It increases by a factor of 4
q.e: Parasite drag is a function of dynamic pressure, which varies with the square of the velocity (V^2). If speed doubles (2), drag increases by two squared (2^2 = 4).

q.t: The drag coefficient...
o: is proportional to the lift coefficient.
may range from zero to an infinite positive value.
cannot be lower than a non-negative, minimal value.
q.e: Even an aerodynamically perfect, frictionless shape at zero lift produces some drag due to air displacement. Thus, the drag coefficient always has a minimum positive base value (CDmin).

q.t: Pressure compensation on an wing occurs at the...
q.e: At the wingtips, the high-pressure air from beneath the wing rolls over the tip to equalize with the low-pressure air on top, creating swirling wingtip vortices (induced drag).

q.t: Which of the following options is likely to produce large induced drag?
q.e: A small aspect ratio means a short, stubby wing. Shorter wings have a proportionally larger wingtip area compared to their span, generating massive, inefficient wingtip vortices and high induced drag.

q.t: Which parts of an aircraft mainly affect the generation of induced drag?
o: the front part of the fuselage.
the outer part of the ailerons.
the lower part of the gear.
q.e: Induced drag is the direct byproduct of lift generation, caused by high-pressure air curling around the wing tips to the low-pressure upper surface, forming vortices.

q.t: Where is interference drag generated?
q.e: Interference drag occurs where two surfaces meet at an angle, such as the wing root joining the fuselage, causing their respective boundary layers to collide and mix turbulently.

q.t: Pressure drag, interference drag and friction drag belong to the group of the...
q.e: Parasite drag is the collective term for all drag not associated with the production of lift. It includes form (pressure) drag, skin friction drag, and interference drag.

q.t: How do induced drag and parasite drag change with increasing airspeed during a horizontal and stable cruise flight?
o: Parasite drag decreases and induced drag increases
Induced drag decreases and parasite drag increases
Parasite drag decreases and induced drag decreases
Induced drag increases and parasite drag increases
q.e: As speed increases, the aircraft flies at a lower angle of attack, reducing wingtip vortices (induced drag decreases). However, flying faster pushes more air out of the way, so parasite drag increases exponentially.

q.t: Which of the listed wing shapes has the lowest induced drag?
q.e: An elliptical wing planform (like the Spitfire) produces an optimal, uniform lift distribution across the entire span, which mathematically results in the absolute minimum induced drag.

q.t: Which effect does a decreasing airspeed have on the induced drag during a horizontal and stable cruise flight?
o: The induced drag will slightly decrease
The induced drag will remain constant
q.e: To maintain horizontal flight as speed decreases, the pilot must increase the angle of attack to generate enough lift. This higher AoA creates stronger wingtip vortices, increasing induced drag.

q.t: Which statement about induced drag during the horizontal cruise flight is correct?
o: Induced drag decreases with increasing airspeed
Induced drag has a minimum at a certain speed and increases at higher as well as lower speeds
Induced drag has a maximum at a certain speed and decreases at higher as well as lower speeds
Induced drag increases with increasing airspeed
q.e: Induced drag is a byproduct of high angles of attack. As airspeed increases, the required angle of attack to maintain lift drops, making the wing more efficient and reducing induced drag.

q.t: Which kinds of drag contribute to total drag?
o: Induced drag, form drag, skin-friction drag
Form drag, skin-friction drag, interference drag
q.e: Total aerodynamic drag is the mathematical sum of Induced Drag (drag from creating lift) and Parasite Drag (drag from simply moving the aircraft's shape through the air).

q.t: How do lift and drag change when approaching a stall condition?
q.e: As the angle of attack approaches the critical stall point, boundary layer separation begins. This destroys the low-pressure lift-generating area while massively increasing turbulent profile drag.

q.t: In case of a stall it is important to...
o: increase the angle of attack and increase the speed.
decrease the angle of attack and increase the speed.
increase the angle of attack and reduce the speed.
increase the bank angle and reduce the speed.
q.e: To recover from a stall, you must re-attach the smooth airflow over the wings. This requires pushing the stick forward to decrease the angle of attack, allowing the aircraft to dive and regain airspeed.

q.t: During a stall, the lift...
q.e: In a full stall, airflow separation destroys the aerodynamic lift over the upper wing, while the broadside presentation of the wing to the wind creates massive pressure drag.

q.t: The critical angle of attack...
o: decreases with forward center of gravity position.
increases with backward center of gravity position.
q.e: A wing will always stall at the exact same critical angle of attack regardless of airspeed, weight, bank angle, or load factor. It is purely an aerodynamic property of the airfoil shape.

q.t: What leads to a decreased stall speed Vs (IAS)?
q.e: Stall speed is proportional to aircraft weight. A lighter aircraft requires less lift to fly, so it can fly slower before needing to reach the critical angle of attack.

q.t: Which statement regarding a spin is correct?
o: During recovery the ailerons should be kept neutral
During the spin the speed constantly increases
During recovery the ailerons should be crossed
Only very old aeroplanes have a risk of spinning
q.e: Applying ailerons during a spin changes the angle of attack differentially on the wings, which can worsen the spin or flatten it out. Ailerons must be strictly neutral during spin recovery.

q.t: The laminar boundary layer on the aerofoil is located between...
o: the stagnation point and the center of pressure.
the stagnation point and the transition point.
the transition point and the separation point.
the transition point and the center of pressure.
q.e: The laminar boundary layer begins precisely at the leading edge (stagnation point) where the air is perfectly smooth, and lasts until the transition point, where it breaks down into turbulence.

q.t: What types of boundary layers can be found on an aerofoil?
o: Laminar boundary layer along the complete upper surface with non-separated airflow
Turbulent layer at the leading wing areas, laminar boundary layer at the trailing areas
Turbulent boundary layer along the complete upper surface with separated airflow
Laminar layer at the leading wing areas, turbulent boundary layer at the trailing areas
q.e: Airflow starts smooth (laminar) at the leading edge. Due to friction and adverse pressure gradients moving aft, it eventually transitions into a thicker, chaotic turbulent boundary layer.

q.t: How does a laminar boundary layer differ from a turbulent boundary layer?
o: The laminar boundary layer is thinner and provides more skin-friction drag
The turbulent boundary layer can follow the airfoil camber at higher angles of attack
The laminar boundary layer produces lift, the turbulent boundary layer produces drag
The turbulent boundary layer is thicker and provides less skin-friction drag
q.e: Although it creates more friction, the turbulent boundary layer has more kinetic energy. This energy allows it to adhere to the wing's curve at high angles of attack, delaying a stall.

q.t: What structural item provides lateral stability to an airplane?
q.e: Wing dihedral (the upward V-angle of the wings) creates a self-correcting rolling moment. If the plane drops a wing, the lower wing generates more vertical lift, rolling the plane level.

q.t: Which statement describes a situation of static stability?
o: An aircraft distorted by external impact will return to the original position
An aircraft distorted by external impact will tend to an even more deflected position
An aircraft distorted by external impact will maintain the deflected position
An aircraft distorted by external impact can return to its original position by rudder input
q.e: Positive static stability means that if an aircraft is disturbed from steady flight (e.g., by a gust), it will naturally and inherently tend to return to its original attitude without pilot input.

q.t: Which constructive feature is shown in the figure? (PFA-006)
q.e: The image demonstrates how an upward angle of the wings from root to tip (dihedral) generates a restoring lift vector when banking, providing positive lateral (roll) stability.

q.t: Longitudinal stability is referred to as stability around which axis?
q.e: Longitudinal stability (pitch stability) dictates the aircraft's tendency to return to level flight after the nose pitches up or down. Pitch occurs around the lateral (wingtip-to-wingtip) axis.

q.t: Stability around which axis is mainly influenced by the center of gravity's longitudinal position?
q.e: The fore-and-aft position of the Center of Gravity dictates how nose-heavy or tail-heavy the aircraft is, directly controlling pitch stability, which is rotation around the lateral axis.

q.t: What structural item provides directional stability to an airplane?
q.e: Directional stability (yaw stability) prevents the aircraft from flying sideways. The vertical tail acts like the feathers on an arrow, forcing the nose to point into the relative wind.

q.t: Rotation around the vertical axis is called...
q.e: Yaw is the side-to-side movement of the aircraft's nose, rotating around the vertical axis passing straight down through the center of gravity. It is controlled by the rudder.

q.t: Rotation around the lateral axis is called...
q.e: Pitch is the up-and-down movement of the aircraft's nose, rotating around the lateral axis that runs from wingtip to wingtip. It is controlled by the elevator.

q.t: The critical angle of attack...
o: increases with a front centre of gravity.
is changed by different aircraft weights.
is not changed by different aircraft weights.
decreases with a rear centre of gravity.
q.e: The critical angle of attack is an aerodynamic constant for a given airfoil shape. Regardless of how heavy the aircraft is, the wing will always stall at the exact same angle.

q.t: In straight and level flight with constant performance of the engine, the angle of attack at the wing is...
q.e: To climb, the aircraft must generate excess lift to overcome gravity, which requires a higher angle of attack. In level flight, less lift is required, so the AoA is smaller.

q.t: What is the function of the horizontal tail (among other things)?
o: To stabilise the aeroplane around the longitudinal axis
To stabilise the aeroplane around the lateral axis
To initiate a curve around the vertical axis
To stabilise the aeroplane around the vertical axis
q.e: The horizontal stabilizer acts like the feathers on an arrow in the vertical plane, providing longitudinal stability, which controls pitch movement around the lateral axis.

q.t: The elevator moves an aeroplane around the...
q.e: The elevator is hinged on the horizontal tail. Moving it pitches the nose up or down, which is a rotation around the lateral axis (running wingtip to wingtip).

q.t: What has to be considered with regard to the center of gravity position?
o: By moving the elevator trim tab, the center of gravity can be shifted into a correct position.
Only correct loading can assure a correct and safe center of gravity position.
The center of gravity's position can only be determined during flight.
By moving the aileron trim tab, the center of gravity can be shifted into a correct position.
q.e: The CG is a physical reality based on the mass distribution of the aircraft. Trim tabs only relieve aerodynamic control forces; they cannot physically move the aircraft's center of gravity.

q.t: Rudder deflections result in a turn of the aeroplane around the...
q.e: The rudder deflects left or right, pushing the tail sideways. This causes the nose to swing left or right (yaw), which is rotation around the vertical axis.

q.t: Deflecting the rudder to the left causes...
o: pitching of the aircraft to the left.
yawing of the aircraft to the left.
pitching of the aircraft to the right.
yawing of the aircraft to the right.
q.e: Pressing the left rudder pedal deflects the rudder surface to the left, pushing the tail to the right, which forces the aircraft's nose to yaw to the left.

q.t: What is the advantage of differential aileron movement?
o: The drag of the downwards deflected aileron is lowered and the adverse yaw is smaller
The total lift remains constant during aileron deflection
The ratio of the drag coefficient to lift coefficient is increased
q.e: In a differential system, the up-going aileron travels further than the down-going aileron. This reduces the drag on the outside wing, mitigating the tendency for the nose to yaw away from the turn (adverse yaw).

q.t: Which design feature can compensate for adverse yaw?
q.e: Differential ailerons, Frise-type ailerons, and coordinated rudder input are the primary engineering and piloting methods used to counter adverse yaw during roll.

q.t: Differential aileron deflection is used to...
o: avoid a stall at low angles of attack.
q.e: By limiting the downward travel of the aileron on the lifting wing, differential ailerons prevent massive induced drag buildup, thereby keeping adverse yaw to a minimum.

q.t: The right aileron deflects upwards, the left downwards. How does the aircraft react?
o: Rolling to the left, no yawing
Rolling to the right, yawing to the left
Rolling to the left, yawing to the right
Rolling to the right, yawing to the right
q.e: Right aileron up reduces lift on the right wing (rolls right). Left aileron down increases lift and induced drag on the left wing, pulling the nose left (adverse yaw).

q.t: The aerodynamic rudder balance...
q.e: Aerodynamic balancing uses air pressure (via a horn, inset hinge, or balance tab) extending forward of the hinge line to help push the control surface, reducing the physical force the pilot feels.

q.t: Which constructive feature has the purpose to reduce stearing forces?
q.e: Aerodynamic balance (like a horn balance on an elevator or rudder) utilizes the airflow catching the front of the control surface to assist the pilot in moving the rear of the surface.

q.t: What is the function of the static rudder balance?
o: To trim the controls almost without any force
To increase the control stick forces
To limit the control stick forces
q.e: Static balance involves adding physical lead weights ahead of the hinge line. This balances the surface's mass, completely preventing high-speed aerodynamic flutter that could destroy the tail.

q.t: The trim tab at the elevator is defelected upwards. In which position is the corresponding indicator?
q.e: If the trim tab goes UP, aerodynamic forces push the main elevator DOWN. A downward elevator pushes the tail up, causing the nose to pitch DOWN. Thus, the indicator shows nose-down trim.

q.t: What describes "wing loading"?
q.e: Wing loading is a critical performance metric defined as the total weight of the aircraft divided by the total surface area of its wings (e.g., kg/m^2 or lbs/sq ft).

q.t: Through which factor listed below does the load factor increase during cruise flight?
q.e: An upward gust suddenly and violently increases the angle of attack on the wings. This massive, instant increase in lift briefly but significantly multiplies the G-forces (load factor) on the airframe.

q.t: Point number 1 in the figure indicates which flight state? (PFA-008)
q.e: On a standard V-n (velocity-load factor) diagram, point 1 sits in the negative G region, representing the structural and aerodynamic limits during negative-G maneuvers or inverted flight.

q.t: Point number 5 in the figure indicates which flight state? (PFA-008)
q.e: Point 5 on the left boundary of the normal flight envelope (positive G region) represents the normal stall speed (Vs1) at 1G, marking the absolute lower limit of slow flight.

q.t: In a co-ordinated turn, how is the relation between the load factor (n) and the stall speed (Vs)?
o: n is smaller than 1, Vs is greater than in straight and level flight.
n is greater than 1, Vs is smaller than in straight and level flight.
n is greater than 1, Vs is greater than in straight and level flight.
n is smaller than 1, Vs is smaller than in straight and level flight.
q.e: To maintain altitude in a turn, back pressure is applied, increasing the load factor (G-force > 1). This "effective weight" requires a higher angle of attack, resulting in an increased stall speed.

q.t: How is the balance of forces affected during a turn?
o: A lower lift force compensates for a lower net force as compared to level flight
Lift force must be increased to compensate for the sum of centrifugal and gravitational force
The horizontal component of the lift force during a turn is the centrifugal force
The net force results from superposition of gravity and centripetal forces
q.e: When banked, a portion of lift pulls the aircraft horizontally. To keep from losing altitude, total lift must be increased so the vertical component equals gravity, overcoming the combined load factor.

q.t: During approch to the next updraft, the vertical speed indicator reads 3 m/s descent. Within the updraft you expect a mean rate of climb of 2 m/s. According McCready, how should you adjust the speed during approach of the updraft?
o: The McCready ring should be set to 2 m/s, the recommended speed can be read at the McCready scale next to the sum of current rate of descent at expected rate of climb (5 m/s).
The McCready ring should be set to 3 m/s, the recommended speed can be read at the McCready scale next to the expected rate of climb (2 m/s).
The McCready ring should be set to 2 m/s, the recommended speed can be read at the McCready scale next to the current rate of descent (3 m/s).
Outside of thermal cells, the McCready ring should be set to 0 m/s, the recommended speed can be read at the McCready scale next to the current rate of descent (3 m/s).
q.e: MacCready theory dictates setting the ring to the anticipated climb rate of the next thermal (2 m/s), and then flying the speed indicated opposite the glider's current sink rate (3 m/s) to maximize cross-country speed.

q.t: A sailplane is operated with additional water ballast. How do best gliding angle and speed of best glide change, when compared to flying without water ballast?
o: best gliding angle descreases, best glide speed decreases.
best gliding angle remains unchanged, best glide speed increases.
best gliding angle remains increases, best glide speed increases.
best gliding angle remains unchanged, best glide speed decreases.
q.e: Adding mass (water ballast) shifts the entire polar curve to the right. The glider achieves the exact same maximum glide ratio, but does so at a significantly higher true airspeed.

q.t: What has to be considered when operating a sailplane with water ballast?
o: It should stay below freezing level.
q.e: Water ballast must be jettisoned before climbing above the freezing level. If water freezes inside the wings, it can destroy the internal structures and jam control linkages.

q.t: What has to be considered when operating a sailplane equipped with camper flaps?
o: During approach and landing, camber must not be changed from negative to positive.
During approach and landing, camber must not be changed from positive to negative.
During winch launch, camber must be set to full negative.
During winch launch, camber must be set to full positive.
q.e: Switching from positive (high lift/drag) to negative (low drag) flaps during a landing approach suddenly drops the lift coefficient, causing the glider to instantly sink or slam into the ground.

q.t: Extending airbrakes results in ...
