q.e: Airbrakes (spoilers) disrupt the smooth aerodynamic flow over the top of the wing. This intentionally destroys a large portion of lift while generating massive profile drag, allowing steep descents.

q.t: The pressure compensation between wind upper and lower surface results in ...
o: induced drag by wing tip vortices.
laminar airflow by wing tip vortices.
profile drag by wing tip vortices.
q.e: The high pressure beneath the wing spills over the tip to the low-pressure upper surface, creating a spiraling vortex of air that trails behind the wing. This energy loss is the primary cause of induced drag.

q.t: What engine design at a Touring Motor Glider (TMG) results in least drag?
o: Engine and propeller mounted fix on the fuselage.
Engine and propeller mounted stowable on the fuselage
Engine and propeller mounted fix at the aircraft's nose
Engine and propeller mounted fix at the horizontal stabilizer
q.e: A stowable (retractable) engine and propeller fold completely into the fuselage and are covered by doors, restoring the glider's clean aerodynamic profile and practically eliminating engine parasite drag.

q.t: At stationary glide and the same mass, what is the difference when using a thick airfoild instead of a thinner airfoil?
q.e: To sustain a stationary glide at the same mass, both airfoils must generate exactly the same lift (to equal weight). However, the thicker airfoil presents a larger frontal area, inherently producing more profile/form drag.

q.t: What is shown by a profile polar?
o: ratio between minimum rate of descent and best glide
ratio between total lift and drag depending on angle of attack
ratio of cA and cD at different angles of attack
lift coefficient cA at different angles of attack
q.e: A profile polar (or drag polar) is a fundamental aerodynamic graph plotting the lift coefficient (cA/CL) against the drag coefficient (cD/CD) across various angles of attack.

q.t: The glide ratio of a sailplane can be improved by which measures?
o: higher airplane mass, thin airfoil, taped gaps between wing and fuselage
lower airplane mass, correct speed, retractable gear
Cleaning, correct speed, retractable gear, taped gaps between wing and fuselage
forward C.G. position, correct speed, taped gaps between wing and fuselage
q.e: Glide ratio is maximized by minimizing drag. Cleaning bugs off the wings, retracting the gear, flying at the exact optimal speed, and sealing control surface gaps with tape all directly reduce parasite drag.

q.t: What effect is referred to as "adverse yaw"?
o: Aileron operation results in a yaw to the desired side due to less drag at the down-deflected aileron
Rudder operation results in a rolling moment to the opposite side due to more lift generated by the faster moving wing.
Aileron operation results in a yaw to the opposite side due to more drag at the up-deflected aileron
Aileron operation results in a yaw to the opposite side due to more drag at the down-deflected aileron
q.e: When rolling, the down-going aileron creates more lift, which inherently creates more induced drag. This drag pulls the aircraft's nose away from the direction of the intended turn (adverse yaw).

q.t: What is meant by "ground effect"?
o: Decrease of lift and increase of induced drag close to the ground
Increase of lift and decrease of induced drag close to the ground
Increase of lift and increase of induced drag close to the ground
Decrease of lift and decrease of induced drag close to the ground
q.e: When flying within one wingspan of the surface, the ground physically blocks the full formation of wingtip vortices. This drastic reduction in induced drag makes the aircraft seem to "float" with increased lift efficiency.

q.t: What is the diffeence between spin and spiral dive?
o: Spin: stall at inner wing, speed increasing rapidly; Spiral dive: airflow at both wings, speed constant
Spin: stall at inner wing, speed constant; Spiral dive: airflow at both wings, speed increasing rapidly
Spin: stall at outer wing, speed constant; Spiral dive: airflow at both wings, speed increasing rapidly
Spin: stall at outer wing, speed increasing rapidly; Spiral dive: airflow at both wings, speed constant
q.e: A spin is an autorotation following an asymmetric stall; the aircraft falls vertically at a relatively constant, low airspeed. A spiral dive is a steep, non-stalled turn where airspeed increases rapidly and dangerously.
